Hand-wrought silver spoon - The Theory of the Leisure Class, Chapter Six: some ten to twenty dollars
Machine-made aluminium spoon - The Theory of the Leisure Class, Chapter Six: some ten to twenty cents

The hand-wrought silver spoon is priced at ten to twenty dollars, while the machine-made aluminium spoon costs only ten to twenty cents—roughly a hundredfold difference in value.

Island - starting population: about seven millions
Island - after fifty years (two periods of twenty-five years): population twenty-eight millions; means of subsistence equal to the support of twenty-one millions

Malthus starts with about seven millions; after fifty years the population would be twenty-eight millions while subsistence would support only twenty-one millions, leaving a shortfall of seven millions.

Yes, force is allowed in the bridge case. According to Chapter V (Applications), if a public officer or anyone else sees a person attempting to cross a bridge ascertained to be unsafe, and there is no time to warn him, they may seize him and turn him back. This does not really infringe his liberty because liberty consists in doing what one desires, and he does not desire to fall into the river. However, when there is only a danger of mischief rather than certainty, no one but the person himself can judge the sufficiency of the motive for incurring the risk, so (unless he is a child, delirious, or in some state of excitement or absorption incompatible with the full use of the reflecting faculty) he ought only to be warned of the danger, not forcibly prevented (Chapter V). Finally, Mill states in Chapter I (Introductory) that the doctrine applies only to human beings in the maturity of their faculties: it does not apply to children or young persons below the legal age, who must be protected against their own actions as well as against external injury.

Principal states of modern Europe - late 18th century: three or four hundred years, or more, to double their numbers
American back settlements - 18th century: fifteen years to double their number

Comparison: 300 ÷ 15 = 20 and 400 ÷ 15 ≈ 27, so the American back settlements doubled roughly 20 to 27 times faster than the principal states of modern Europe.

Veblen concedes the corset impairs the wearer's personal attractions, but this loss is offset by the gain in reputability from her visibly increased expensiveness and infirmity (Chapter Seven, [1]). It has fallen into disuse among the richest class because a leisure class has grown up wealthy enough that any aspersion about enforced manual employment would be idle and harmless calumny, so the corset's evidence is no longer needed (Chapter Seven, [5], [4]). It persists among the later accessions of the wealthy classes—such as recently enriched American cities—who have not yet divested themselves of the plebeian canons of taste carried over from their former lower pecuniary grade, and it continues wherever it serves as evidence of honorific leisure by arguing physical disability in the wearer (Chapter Seven, [4], [2]).

1st edition (1859) - elephant estimate: breeds at thirty years old, breeds till ninety, bringing forth three pair of young in this interval; at the end of the fifth century there would be alive fifteen million elephants descended from the first pair.
6th edition (1872) - elephant estimate: begins breeding when thirty years old, breeds till ninety, bringing forth six young in the interval, and surviving till one hundred years old; after a period of from 740 to 750 years there would be nearly nineteen million elephants alive descended from the first pair.

Between editions, Darwin changed the assumption from three pair (six young) to six young and added survival to one hundred years old; the result changed from fifteen million elephants at the end of the fifth century to nearly nineteen million elephants after 740 to 750 years.

Darwin calls it the doctrine of Malthus applied to the whole animal and vegetable kingdoms [5], [7].

According to Malthus's own Essay:
- Population, when unchecked, increases in a geometrical ratio, while subsistence increases only in an arithmetical ratio (Chapter 1) [1], [10].
- Because these powers are unequal, a strong and constantly operating check on population arises from the difficulty of subsistence (Chapter 1) [1].
- Taking the United States as actual experience, Malthus adopts as his rule that unchecked population doubles every twenty-five years, i.e., increases in a geometrical ratio (Chapter 2) [2].

Mill - On Liberty: Society itself can tyrannise beyond political functionaries, imposing "its own ideas and practices as rules of conduct on those who dissent from them" through prevailing opinion and feeling, penetrating "much more deeply into the details of life, and enslaving the soul itself" [1][7].

Tocqueville - Democracy in America: The majority's power reaches through public opinion, the legislature, the executive, the troops, the jury, and even elected judges, so that the wronged individual finds "no sure barrier" and no avenue of redress; its effects are felt "more sensibly... in the manners than in the conduct of society," checking the development of leading characters [3][6][8].

Comparison: Mill sees the deepest danger as social tyranny—the majority's moral and opinion-based pressure on individual thought and self-regarding conduct, which leaves fewer means of escape than political oppression [1][10]. Tocqueville sees the danger as the majority's overpowering strength across all institutions and manners, leaving inadequate securities against tyranny even where laws mitigate it [6][8]. Both agree the threat extends beyond laws and officials into opinion itself, but Mill stresses enslavement of the soul through social conformity, while Tocqueville stresses the majority's unchecked institutional and moral dominance in America.

Malthus - rule for unchecked population: doubling every twenty-five years (geometrical ratio)
Tocqueville - United States population: 1790, 3,929,328; 1830, 12,856,165
Tocqueville - own statement: the population "had more than tripled in the space of forty years"

Malthus's rule implies roughly a fourfold (two doublings) in fifty years; Tocqueville's figures show more than a tripling in forty years (12,856,165 ÷ 3,929,328 ≈ 3.3), which is consistent with a doubling period somewhat longer than twenty-five years. Tocqueville himself gives no explicit doubling period, only that the population more than tripled in forty years.

On Liberty (Mill) - United States: the feeling of the majority, to whom any appearance of a more showy or costly style of living than they can hope to rival is disagreeable, operates as a tolerably effectual sumptuary law, and in many parts of the Union it is really difficult for a person possessing a very large income to find any mode of spending it which will not incur popular disapprobation.
The Theory of the Leisure Class (Veblen) - standard of living: the accepted standard of expenditure in the community or class largely determines a person's standard of living, directly through common sense and indirectly through popular insistence on conformity to the accepted scale of expenditure as a matter of propriety, under pain of disesteem and ostracism; the want is indefinitely expansible, so increased output goes to meeting it.

Mill describes majority feeling in the United States acting as an effective sumptuary law that makes showy spending by the very rich incur popular disapprobation; Veblen's theory explains the restrained motive as the drive to conform to (and expand along) the accepted pecuniary standard of expenditure, enforced by fear of disesteem and ostracism.
